item.title: Red Sox Should Consider Predicted $118M Pitcher if Sonny Gray Leaves in Free Agency
item.description: Red Sox Should Consider Predicted $118M Pitcher if Sonny Gray Leaves in Free Agency originally appeared on NESN . Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here . With the possibility of losing right-hander Sonny Gray in MLB free agency, the Boston Red Sox will have to figure out who they want to replace him with. The reality is that there aren’t many great starting pitchers available in Major League Baseball this offseason, and teams like the Red Sox will have to consider that. However, one player makes a ton of sense for Boston: right-hander Michael King. King is a Northeast guy, went to school at Northeastern, and has played for the New York Yankees throughout his career. All of those factors make him a perfect candidate to join a team like the Red Sox, though his contract situation does lead to some questions. King is expected to land a deal worth over $100 million, with the latest prediction recently suggesting that he could be a four-year, $118 million man. However, it was also noted that he really enjoys his time with the San Diego Padres. “I expect King to opt out of the two remaining player-option years on his contract so he can receive a $5 million buyout and then look to secure a long-term contract. King had a terrific year with the Padres, posting a 3.21 ERA in 185 innings over 32 starts. He’s from the East Coast but has really enjoyed his time with the Padres, considers San Diego his second home and has sincere interest in staying. San Diego desperately needs to re-sign him, as he’s clearly the ace of their staff,” Jim Bowden said . With King now a free agent, baseball expects he'll at least listen to other teams around the league. He's coming off a ridiculous postseason, showing that he has the stuff to be among the best in baseball at any given moment. He was perhaps better than anybody in the playoffs this year, appearing in three games, starting two of them, and posting a 0.64 ERA in 14.0 innings. item.title: 10 takeaways from Oregon State’s loss at Fresno State
item.description: FRESNO, Calif. — Oregon State lost to Fresno State 38-22 Saturday night at Valley Children’s Stadium. Here are 10 takeaways as the Beavers prepare to host Texas State. 1. Reality check Two things can be true. Oregon State can still be ahead of schedule and on its way to a legitimately surprising season amid a massive rebuild, complete with a potent offense. Much of its success thus far came by pounding less talented teams and several of the worst defenses in the country. And where OSU was vulnerable was there to be exploited by teams like Fresno State, which has talent and good coaching. The Beavers are not a College Football Playoff team. That dose of reality doesn’t diminish what’s being accomplished this season. They’re simply not one of the two most talented teams in the Pac-12 right now. 2. Oregon State was outcoached JaMarcus Shephard and his staff were outcoached for definitely the first time in conference play and arguably for the first time this season. Matt Entz laid out in detail what Fresno State picked up from studying Braden Atkinson from his time at Mercer and Oregon State’s tendencies. Bye weeks also include self-scouting. Fresno State was more prepared for what OSU showed and particularly offensively the Beavers did not have an effective counter. 3. Self-inflicted errors can’t happen in games like this Winning on the road against a team with at least comparable (if not better) talent and coaching is a difficult task to begin with. It becomes a whole lot harder with six presnap penalties and allowing five sacks with two leading to fumbles. OSU absolutely could have led by multiple scores early if not for a false start negating Jake Reichle’s would-be touchdown, if Aeryn Hampton’s foot was in bounds and if multiple other penalties didn’t occur. That doesn’t even get into defensive miscues from missed tackles or over-pursuits. 4. The offensive line may have had its worst game Houston was more physically dominating than Fresno State, but that’s to be expected. Oregon State’s offensive line had a brutal showing nearly across the board, with sacks allowed by multiple players in one-on-one matchups. OSU’s rushing stats are skewed by the sacks and not nearly as poor as the final box score, but the bottom line is Fresno State won the line of scrimmage and it’s not a particularly stout group. 5. Josiah Freeman was the best receiver on the field Fresno State’s 6-foot-4 receiver had a big night with two touchdowns. Freeman had a massive advantage against Isaiah Houi and performed accordingly. If there’s one piece OSU’s receiving corps is missing it is a target with the size and length of Freeman, which the Beavers are leaning on via their tight ends. But an outside target like him is hard to beat and he showed why. 6. item.title: Houston Rockets jersey history No. 40 - Dick Gibbs (1971-72)
item.description: The Houston Rockets have had players donning a total of 52 different jersey numbers (and have one not part of any numerical series for Houston assistant coach and general manager Carroll Dawson) since their founding at the start of the 1967-68 season, worn by just under 500 players in the course of Rockets history. To honor all of the players who wore those numbers over the decades, Rockets Wire is covering the entire history of jersey numbers and the players who wore them since the founding of the team all those years ago right up to the present day. With seven of those jerseys now retired to honor some of the greatest Rockets of all time to wear those jerseys, there is a lot of history to cover. And for today's article, we will continue with the first of eight who wore the No. 40, Dick Gibbs. After ending his college career at Texas-El Paso, Gibbs was picked up with the 49th overall selection of the 1971 NBA Draft by the Chicago Bulls. The Ames, Iowa native played the first 2 seasons of his pro career with the Houston Rockets instead, coming to an end when he had his contract sold to the (then) Kansas City-Omaha (now, Sacramento) Kings in 1972. During his time suiting up for the Rockets, Gibbs wore only jersey No. 40 and put up 3.7 points and 2.2 rebounds per game. All stats and data courtesy of Basketball Reference. item.title: Matt Barrie: Final month of CFB season will be ‘tipping point’ that dictates ‘next 10 years’
item.description: Credit: The Matt Barrie Show Many college football commentators have already declared the 2026 season among the best of all time, and it could cement itself as such this weekend if Notre Dame-Miami, BYU-Utah, Alabama-LSU, and several other games live up to expectations. After that, rivalry week and conference championship season will only add to the fireworks heading into the College Football Playoff. It’s enough for ESPN’s Matt Barrie to declare the final month of the college football season a “tipping point” for the sport that will shift how it is run and covered for the next decade or more. “We have four weekends left in the regular season … the schedule-makers did their job because they’re giving us an all-time weekend in the first weekend of November,” he said Sunday on his podcast , The Matt Barrie Show. “And then little by little, this last four weeks of the regular season, the ball that we’re about to see is going to be one of those months … that we look back on at the end of the season and next year and the year after, we’re going to look at this as a tipping point in college football. “Because we’ve been saying it all year, parity, NIL has flattened out rosters. And now we’re at the new norm, and how this thing plays out over the next four years could dictate how we approach this sport for the next 10 years. Because if Wake Forest goes on another run and pulls an Indiana, what are we doing with these Blue Bloods? I’m trying to find schools that historically have nothing, and because of the way college football is now, have everything.” This week the CFP committee will also announce its first weekly rankings during a primetime broadcast on ESPN. Barrie pleaded with the committee to do the hard work of evaluating teams’ performance rather than resorting to standings and head-to-head results. “Now we get to the point where we think, based on the matchups, it’ll be settled on the field,” he said. “And I say we think that because every time you think it matters on the field, the committee will come out and do something to completely throw that away. I just hope, I really hope — because we’re going to 24 — and I hope that within this 12, they dig in and they watch and they look and they see. Because you’ve gotta get this right. Because we’ve been handed the greatest season of all time, and the last thing we need is a room of committee members to screw it up.” A season defined by upsets and chaos still needs a champion. And college football is such that the champion will, in part, be chosen subjectively. Barrie’s larger point that the results of this season will change the sport is worth considering. Even if a Cinderella like Wake Forest doesn’t shock the world, NCAA and conference leadership has to be taking note of the parity among schools and conferences, and especially the value of the regular season as an entertainment product and a way to determine excellence. item.title: How Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer performed in their first events as world number one
item.description: Alexander Zverev became the 30th official world number one on Monday. Zverev snatched the top spot from Jannik Sinner after defeating Tallon Griekspoor in the Vienna Open round of 16 last week. Zverev is now set to compete in the Paris Masters – his first tournament as world number one. With Zverev assuming the top spot, let’s take a look back at how some of tennis’ greatest players performed upon achieving world number one status. Novak Djokovic won the Canadian Open Djokovic claimed the world number one ranking from Rafael Nadal after defeating Frenchman Jo-Wilfried Tsonga in the 2011 Wimbledon semi-finals. “They don’t give you a lot of chances to become number one,” Djokovic said afterwards with a smile. “I guess you need to lose only one match in seven months to get there.” The Serb went on to win his first title at the All England Club, beating Nadal in the final. Djokovic carried his excellent form to Montreal, defeating Nikolay Davydenko, Marin Cilic, Gael Monfils, Jo-Wilfried Tsonga and Mardy Fish en route to the title. In securing the title, Djokovic became the first player to win five Masters 1000 events [since the format alteration in 2009]. “History-making, of course it’s special,” Djokovic said after beating Fish in the final. “Of course, it’s an honour and privilege to be part of the history of the sport that I love and that I play.” Rafael Nadal lost to Andy Murray at the US Open Nadal achieved the world number one ranking after winning gold at the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing. The Spaniard, who defeated Chile’s Fernando Gonzalez in the gold-medal match, overtook Roger Federer to claim the top spot. “That year [2008], Novak started to play so well. For me it was another tough rival, so I thought, well, I have been there [at the top level], but I didn’t achieve the world number one. Now another great player is coming, so maybe I will never be No. 1,” Nadal told the ATP in 2025. Photo by Clive Brunskill/Getty Images “So for me that’s why it was so important for me to achieve that. I believe that I deserved it after having a very high level almost in every week during three and a half years.” After assuming the number one ranking, Nadal competed in the US Open. The Spaniard defeated Sam Querrey and Mardy Fish en route to the semi-finals, before losing to Andy Murray in four sets. Roger Federer helped Swiss win their Davis Cup tie Federer debuted as world number one after defeating Juan Carlos Ferrero in the 2004 Australian Open semi-finals. item.title: The Cadillac F1 Team is For Sale – If You Have $3 Billion
item.description: Rumors have been swirling for months and now it appears, where there's smoke, there's fire. And we're not just talking about the Cadillac F1 team's brake issues. Mark Walter is reportedly exploring a sale of his Cadillac Formula 1 stake, with an asking price of no less than $3 billion and at least seven interested parties, according to three people familiar with the process. The team is wrapping up its debut F1 season, and despite an even worse than anticipated campaign, that doesn't seem to have had any impact on the valuation. Walter controls the team through TWG Global, which houses his racing holdings in F1, IndyCar, and NASCAR under its TWG Motorsports division. The operation is run jointly with General Motors and its Cadillac subsidiary. TWG holds controlling ownership, although the split between the partners has not been disclosed. The firm had not responded to inquiries about the sale. The move would reverse a position TWG stated plainly just last month. Once Walter agreed to sell the Los Angeles Lakers to Joshua Kushner and Bob Iger for $12.5 billion, the firm ruled out any sale of the Cadillac F1 team or MLB's Los Angeles Dodgers. "TWG is not considering exiting its stake in the Cadillac Formula 1 team or any other part of TWG Motorsports," the firm said in a long statement. That statement addressed speculation about Walter's sports portfolio after he drew scrutiny over undisclosed related-party dealings at insurance companies he controls through Guggenheim Partners, the firm he co-founded and leads as CEO. The nondisclosures spurred two federal investigations. Walter has also sold his 13% stake in Chelsea to Clearlake Capital, and he is reportedly seeking a buyer for the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks at $700 million. item.title: Shane Wright Clearly Wanted Out Of Seattle
item.description: Shane Wright may not be willing to say he asked the Seattle Kraken for a trade, but his first comments as a member of the Nashville Predators suggest he was ready for a change. The 22-year-old forward met with reporters Monday after Seattle dealt him to Nashville in exchange for Matthew Wood. When asked whether he and his representatives had requested a move, Wright gave an answer that left a little room for interpretation. “I wouldn’t say, like, we requested a trade,” Wright said speaking to Predators beat reporter Alex Daugherty. “I think for me, I just always wanted a little more opportunity, I wanted to have more minutes, wanted to play a bigger role. Whether that was in Seattle or somewhere else, I was happy to do that. But now (I’m) moving on from that situation, and I’m happy to be here.” There's a distinction worth pointing out. Wright didn't come out and say he demanded a trade, nor did he flat-out deny that a request was made. What he did acknowledge was that his situation in Seattle wasn't giving him the opportunity he wanted. Whether that meant a bigger role with the Kraken or a fresh start somewhere else, he was ready for something different. And it's not as if the possibility of Wright leaving Seattle came out of nowhere. Back in July, Sportsnet's Elliotte Friedman reported that Wright's agent, Kurt Overhardt, had indicated the two sides had reached an understanding about finding the young forward a new home. Overhardt specifically said Kraken general manager Jason Botterill had agreed to move Wright during the offseason, with the goal of finding him a team in need of a young center. “I can confirm that we have had positive conversations with GM Jason Botterill, and he has agreed to move Shane this summer to a team in need of a top young center,” Overhardt said at the time, per Friedman. Botterill declined to comment on the situation when asked by Friedman. The trade eventually came Sunday, with Seattle and Nashville swapping two former first-round picks in a one-for-one deal. Wright heads to the Predators, while Wood gets a fresh opportunity with the Kraken. For Wright, the move comes after a difficult stretch in Seattle. Once projected to go No. 1 overall in the 2022 NHL Draft, he fell to the Kraken at No. 4. He made his NHL debut as an 18-year-old in 2022, but never quite developed into the top-line centerpiece Seattle had hoped he could become. He finished the 2025-26 season with 27 points (including 12 goals and 15 assists) in 74 games, down considerably from the 44 points he recorded in 79 appearances the previous season. He also had four points, including three goals, through 14 games this season before the trade. Wood, meanwhile, arrives in Seattle with a different profile.
